11-1.question: You are sizing up an opening 13-tile hand before choosing a direction. Which counts are worth making?
options: How many pairs you hold
How many tiles already sit in a run shape
How many completely isolated tiles you hold
How many Faan your finished hand will score
11-1.explanation: Pairs, run shapes and isolated tiles decide which directions are even possible, while the final Faan value is unknown at the start.

11-1.question: This 13-tile hand is {{m1}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{p2}}{{p2}}{{p6}}{{p7}}{{s5}}{{s6}}{{s7}}{{east}}{{red}}{{white}}. How many tiles are completely isolated (no pair, no neighbour within two ranks)?
11-1.explanation: {{east}}, {{red}} and {{white}} have no partner and no neighbour, so they are the first tiles to leave.

11-1.question: Match each opening hand shape to the direction it best supports.

pairs.left: Eight Bamboo tiles plus three honour tiles
Four separate pairs spread over three suits
Eleven tiles in one suit and two unrelated tiles
Four finished runs plus a pair

11-1.explanation: The shapes point to the direction: pairs feed Pongs, one long suit feeds flush hands, and finished runs point to 平糊.

11-1.question: Your hand is {{s2}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{s5}}{{s6}}{{s7}}{{s8}}{{east}}{{east}}{{red}}{{m1}}{{p9}}{{p9}} and you are steering toward Mixed One Suit. Which tile should leave first?
options: {{red}}
{{east}}
11-1.explanation: Mixed One Suit keeps one suit plus honours, so the lone tile in an abandoned suit goes first while {{red}} and both pairs still hold meld potential.

11-1.question: You hold {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{p7}}{{p8}}{{p9}}{{s4}}{{s4}}{{s9}}{{east}}{{red}}. How many complete melds do you already have?
options: Two melds, with two more to complete
Three melds, with one more to complete
One meld, with three more to complete
Four melds, so the hand is already complete
11-1.explanation: {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}} and {{p7}}{{p8}}{{p9}} are complete, while {{m5}}{{m6}} is only a shape and {{s4}}{{s4}} is the pair.

11-2.question: Turn 8. You are not going to win this hand. Which moves fit a defensive plan?
options: Accept that the hand is lost and aim to pay nothing
Discard a tile that the dangerous opponent threw this round, before their next draw
Push for a bigger hand to catch up on points
Call every meld you can to change your luck
11-2.explanation: Under 半銃制 the discarder pays the whole amount alone, so a hand you cannot win is best played purely to avoid dealing in.

11-2.question: An opponent has called two Pongs by turn 7. How many more melds must they complete before the hand can win?
11-2.explanation: A winning hand is four melds plus a pair, so two exposed Pongs still leave two melds to go.

11-2.question: Match each mid-game situation to the priority that fits it.

pairs.left: Three melds and a pair in hand by turn 6
One meld and no connected shapes by turn 8
An opponent with three exposed melds barely discards
A draw turns a pair into the triplet you wanted
pairs.right: Commit to the direction it opens

11-2.explanation: Mid-game choices follow the clock: a live hand gets pushed, a dead one gets folded, and a heavy opponent gets respect.

11-2.question: Turn 9. You are one tile from ready, but the wait is the closed shape {{p4}}{{p6}} and the wall is thinning. What is the honest read?
options: You are close, but a one-tile wait may never arrive, so widening it is worth a small cost
You should fold immediately because the wait is closed
A closed wait is as good as a two-sided wait
You should break the pair to stay flexible
11-2.explanation: Being one tile from ready only pays if the tile is live, and a closed wait has at most four copies against up to eight for a two-sided wait.

11-2.question: Turn 7. You are collecting Circles for 混一色 and notice nine Circle tiles already on the table. What does that change?
options: The flush is weaker, because those copies can no longer be drawn
The flush is stronger, because other players are helping you
Nothing, since visible tiles matter only for defence
You must switch to another suit immediately
11-2.explanation: Every visible copy is one fewer left in the wall, so a heavily exposed suit has fewer tiles left to finish the hand.

11-3.question: Which of these are good reasons to PASS on a tile you could claim?
options: Calling would drop 門前清, worth 1 Faan
The call would expose the suit you are collecting
You hold two dragons and the third one is discarded
The call would replace a two-sided wait with a closed wait
11-3.explanation: Passing protects Faan and information, and the dragon case is the opposite one because that claim is worth taking.

11-3.question: Match each claim decision to its main cost or gain.

pairs.left: Pong a discarded dragon while holding two
Chow into the suit of your flush
Chow on your third turn with a concealed hand
Pass on a tile that would complete your third meld

11-3.explanation: Every claim trades something: Faan, information, or speed, so the decision is which of those you can best afford.

11-3.question: You hold two dragons and Pong the third when it is discarded. How many Faan is that triplet worth?
11-3.explanation: A triplet of dragons is 1 Faan, which is why the lesson says to take it when it is offered.

11-3.question: Your hand is {{red}}{{red}}{{east}}{{east}}{{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{p5}}{{p6}}{{p7}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{s9}}. An opponent discards one of the tiles below. Which claim is worth taking?
options: {{red}}
11-3.explanation: The dragon Pong adds 1 Faan and says nothing about your suit, while {{p8}} and {{m1}} would break a finished meld and {{s9}} cannot be claimed at all.

11-3.question: You are playing a concealed hand and hold {{p5}}{{p5}}{{p5}}{{p5}}. Declaring a concealed kong costs you 門前清?
options: No, a concealed kong keeps 門前清 intact
Yes, every kong counts as a claim on the table
Yes, kongs and pongs both break it
Only exposed kongs are allowed in a concealed hand
11-3.explanation: Only a claimed chow, pong or exposed kong breaks 門前清, and an ankan is not a claim.

11-4.question: The sample hand holds {{s3}}{{s4}} as a two-sided wait. Arrange its winning tiles from lowest to highest.
Your hand is {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{m7}}{{p2}}{{p3}}{{s5}}{{s6}}{{s7}}{{east}}{{east}}{{red}}. Which tile should you discard?
options: {{red}}
{{east}}
11-4.explanation: {{red}} is the only tile with no pair and no neighbour, so cutting it leaves three melds, the pair {{east}}{{east}} and the {{p2}}{{p3}} wait.

11-4.question: In the sample opening hand {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m5}}{{m5}}{{p1}}{{p4}}{{p5}}{{p6}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{s7}}{{east}}{{red}}, how many tiles are completely isolated?
11-4.explanation: {{p1}}, {{s7}}, {{east}} and {{red}} have no pair and no neighbour, which is why the lesson discards them before touching any shape.

11-4.question: Three melds are finished and {{m5}}{{m5}} is the pair. Which statements are true from here?
options: One more meld plus the pair finishes the hand
The pair {{m5}}{{m5}} scores Faan on its own
Every discard from here should weigh what the other three players show
Breaking the pair to chase 清一色 is the efficient move
11-4.explanation: The pair is only the eye and adds no Faan, so the remaining work is a fourth meld played with the whole table in view.

11-4.question: Why does the lesson steer this sample hand toward All Chows rather than Mixed One Suit?
options: Its shapes sit in all three suits, so honour-free runs are the cheapest route
All Chows always scores more than Mixed One Suit
Mixed One Suit requires a pair of dragons
All Chows needs only three melds
11-4.explanation: With usable shapes in three suits, chasing one suit would throw most of the hand away, and 平糊 arrives far sooner even at 1 Faan.

11-5.question: Which habits hold up across a whole simulated hand?
options: Plan three discards ahead, not just the current one
Count the tiles still unseen before committing to a wait
Always chase the highest-Faan hand on the table
Re-scan all three opponents before every discard
11-5.explanation: Planning, counting outs and reading the table compound over a hand, while chasing the biggest hand ignores whether it can still arrive.

11-5.question: Match each moment of a hand to the question that should drive it.

pairs.right: Which directions do these shapes support?
Am I still on track, and how fast is the table?
What can this tile deal in to?
What does this call cost in Faan and information?

11-5.explanation: Each phase of a hand has one governing question, and mixing them up is how plans go wrong.

11-5.question: You win a limit hand (例牌) on a discard. How many points does the discarder pay?
11-5.explanation: Every limit hand counts as 10 Faan, and 10 Faan on a discard pays 128.

11-5.question: Which is the strongest reason to abandon a plan mid-hand?
options: The tiles the plan needs are nearly all visible on the table
You have drawn badly for one turn
The plan would score less than 10 Faan
An opponent called a meld
11-5.explanation: Visible tiles cannot be drawn, so a plan whose tiles are gone has no outs left however good it looked at the start.

11-5.question: The hand holds {{p7}}{{p8}}. Arrange the two tiles that complete it from lowest to highest.
11-5.explanation: {{p7}}{{p8}} accepts {{p6}} and {{p9}}, and counting both ends is how a wait's outs are measured.
